quiz: Presentation 3 — Cyber Fraud & the Money Trail: Quiz
structure: 2 case studies × 3 questions + 12 direct questions = 18 questions

scenarios.title: Case study 1 — The refund that went elsewhere
scenarios.scenario: An NRI who has lived in the UK for nearly 50 years filed his return for FY 2023-24 and received his genuine refund. Fraudsters then took over his e-filing account, changed the registered e-mail, mobile number and bank account, and filed a revised return in his name. About ₹2.26 crore of further refund was paid into a fraudulent bank account and moved through several companies’ accounts, with a commission cut at each stage.
scenarios.source: The Tribune, 14 July 2026 (Panchkula Cyber Crime Police)

questions.question: At which point did the Department have its best chance to stop the money?
options: When the mobile, e-mail and bank account were changed just before a large refund on a revised return
When the original return for FY 2023-24 was filed and the first, genuine refund was credited to his account
When each company in the chain deducted its commission before passing the balance to the next account
When the money finally left the last company’s account and was withdrawn in cash by the organisers
questions.explanation: A change of contact details and bank account followed quickly by a large revised-return refund is the red flag. Once the refund leaves, the money moves through layers within hours.

questions.question: Taking over the NRI’s e-filing account and filing a return in his name is, at its core, which offence?
options: Disclosure of taxpayer information by a public servant — Section 494 of the Income-tax Act, 2025
Identity theft and cheating by personation — Sections 66C and 66D IT Act, with cheating under the BNS
Organised crime under Section 111 BNS alone, because the money passed through several companies
No criminal offence, only a tax-recovery matter, because the refund was paid by the Department itself
questions.explanation: Using another person’s password or identity is Section 66C; cheating by impersonating him online is Section 66D, alongside cheating under Sections 318–319 BNS.

questions.question: Which record would most directly show who took over the e-filing account?
options: The NRI’s original return for FY 2023-24 and the refund order issued on it, read with his bank statement
The NRI’s Annual Information Statement, which lists every refund and payment made against his PAN
The e-filing portal’s logs — login IPs and times, OTPs, and changes to e-mail, mobile and bank
Form 26AS of the companies through which the money passed, showing the tax deducted on each payment
questions.explanation: The portal’s logs show when and from where the details were changed; the IP and exact time lead to the subscriber, and the new bank account’s KYC to its holder. Electronic records need a Section 63 BSA certificate.

scenarios.title: Case study 2 — The security guard’s ₹3.91 crore demand
scenarios.scenario: A contractual security guard with no taxable income was assessed for AY 2017-18 on about ₹49.49 crore of cash payments and cash sales shown against his PAN on the portal. The Assessing Officer taxed 8% as income and raised a demand of about ₹3.91 crore, relying only on the portal data. The guard said his PAN had been misused and had complained to the police. The Delhi High Court quashed the assessment.
scenarios.source: Delhi High Court, Lalit v. Union of India, W.P.(C) 9365/2025 (LiveLaw, 14 October 2026)

questions.question: In the session’s terms, what does this profile most suggest?
options: A misused or rented identity — the PAN leads to a front man, not to the person who gained
A large hidden business run by the guard himself, using his job as a cover for cash trading
A simple data-entry error by the reporting company, which needs no further inquiry by the AO
A routine case of under-reported GST turnover, to be referred to the GST authorities at once
questions.explanation: A low-income person shown with crores of transactions is the classic mule or identity-misuse profile. A PAN on a record shows it was quoted, not who used it.

questions.question: Which power should the AO have used to test the portal data before assessing?
options: A notice to the guard’s bank under Section 94 BNSS [old Section 91 CrPC] for his account statements
Referring the case to the police under Section 258 [old Section 138] and waiting for the FIR’s outcome
A search and seizure at the guard’s home as the very first step of the inquiry into the transactions
Calling for information from the company — Section 133(6) of the 1961 Act [now Section 252, 2025 Act]
questions.explanation: The Court said the AO should have made further inquiries, including under Section 133(6). Section 94 BNSS is a police power, not available to a tax officer.

questions.question: Which error did the Court find in the assessment?
options: It taxed only 8% as income, when the whole ₹49.49 crore should have been added as unexplained money
It was made under the 1961 Act, when it should have been made under the Income-tax Act, 2025
It relied only on portal data, withheld the material relied on and ignored the PAN-misuse claim
It was made before the guard had been prosecuted for the transactions recorded under his PAN
questions.explanation: The Court found a breach of natural justice and no independent evidence linking him to the transactions.

questions.question: In a phishing APK fraud, why does the fake app ask the victim for the OTP?
options: So that the bank can confirm the victim’s updated KYC before the deadline
So that the APK file can be unlocked and installed on the victim’s phone
So that the victim’s PAN can be verified with the Income Tax Department
So that the criminal can register the victim’s bank account on his own phone
questions.explanation: The criminal installs the real bank app with the victim’s mobile number; the OTP typed into the fake app reaches his dashboard and ties his handset to the victim’s account.

questions.question: A fraud payment went to a UPI ID ending in ‘@oksbi’. What does the part after ‘@’ tell you?
options: The bank and branch where the receiving account is actually held
The app’s partner (PSP) bank — not necessarily the bank holding the account
The State in which the account holder lives and opened the account
The telecom operator of the mobile number linked to the account
questions.explanation: The handle shows the payment app’s partner bank. Ask that bank or NPCI, with the RRN, which bank holds the account.

questions.question: Which of these will a tax officer NOT see in SFT or AIS data?
options: Cash deposits of ₹10 lakh or more in a year in a savings account
Time deposits above the reporting limit made during the year
Credit-card bill payments above the limit made during the year
Thousands of small UPI credits into a mule’s savings account
questions.explanation: SFT covers large cash deposits, time deposits and card bills — not UPI or IMPS credits. That is why tax data maps mule networks only later.

questions.question: Which power lets an Assessing Officer call for a bank’s or platform’s records on a suspect account?
options: Section 94 BNSS [old Section 91 CrPC], read with Section 168
Section 106 BNSS [old Section 102 CrPC], seizure of property
Section 79 of the IT Act, read with the IT Rules, 2021
Section 252 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 [old Section 133(6)]
questions.explanation: Section 252 is the Department’s own power. Sections 94 and 106 BNSS are police powers; Section 79 IT Act is the intermediaries’ safe harbour.

questions.question: A large transaction appears against a PAN in portal data. On its own, what does that prove?
options: That the PAN holder personally made the transaction
That the PAN holder earned and kept the money
Only that the PAN was quoted for the transaction
That the PAN holder knowingly lent his account
questions.explanation: A PAN, phone number or IP is an identity, not a person. Independent evidence — counterparty records, KYC, logins — must link the person to the transaction (Lalit v. UoI).

questions.question: When must a Section 63 BSA [old Section 65B IEA] certificate accompany an electronic record?
options: Every time the computer output is tendered in evidence
Only when the other side disputes the record in court
Only for records obtained from platforms based abroad
Only when the original device has been lost or destroyed
questions.explanation: Section 63(4) requires the certificate each time; the Supreme Court upheld it in Pune Bar Association v. UoI (22 May 2026).

questions.question: Why is the hash value of seized data recorded at the time of seizure?
options: To show later that the data has not changed since it was seized
To encrypt the data so that the accused can no longer read it
To compress the data so that it fits on the evidence drive
To identify the owner of the device from which it was taken
questions.explanation: A hash is an ‘electronic fingerprint’: any change in the data changes it. A matching hash at trial proves integrity.

questions.question: In a search, a cloud account is locked and the person will not give the password. What does the Income-tax Act, 2025 allow?
options: Nothing — virtual digital space lies outside the scope of a search under the Act
The authorised officer may gain access by overriding the access code (Section 247)
The officer must first obtain a Magistrate’s warrant under Section 94 BNSS
Only the police may open it, after registering an FIR under the IT Act
questions.explanation: Section 247(1)(b)(iii) [old 132(1)(iib)] allows access by overriding the access code where it is not available; Section 261(j) defines virtual digital space.

questions.question: Under the MHA SOP of 2 January 2026, ₹30,000 of one victim is on hold and is not needed for investigation. Who may release it?
options: Only a Magistrate, under Section 503 BNSS [old Section 457 CrPC], after an FIR
The bank on its own, as soon as the victim gives it a written request
The police, under Section 106(3) BNSS, with SP/DCP approval and an indemnity bond
The RBI Ombudsman, on a complaint filed by the victim against the bank
questions.explanation: For a single victim and an amount below ₹50,000, the SOP allows police release after notice to the account holder, approval and an indemnity bond, with a report to the court.

questions.question: What does the new Section 107 BNSS add for victims of cyber fraud?
options: The Magistrate may attach proceeds and share them rateably among victims
Police may freeze any account without reporting the freeze to a Magistrate
Banks must refund every victim within seven days of the complaint
Victims may attach the accused’s house without going to a court
questions.explanation: Section 107 provides for attachment with a Magistrate’s order; Section 107(6) allows rateable distribution among victims through the District Magistrate.

questions.question: A bank’s weak security leads to a customer-data leak. Under the DPDP Act, who faces the penalty, and from when?
options: The employee who leaked it — from 14 November 2025
The bank’s directors personally — from 1 July 2024
No one — the Act has no penalty for such a leak
The bank, as data fiduciary — from 14 May 2027
questions.explanation: Penalties (up to ₹250 crore for failing to take security safeguards) fall on the data fiduciary; most duties and penalties apply from 14 May 2027. Individuals are reached under Section 72A IT Act and the BNS.

questions.question: Fraud money parked in USDT in a mule’s wallet is, for tax purposes, best treated as…
options: A VDA gain taxed at a flat 30% under Section 194
Unexplained money, not a gain on a virtual digital asset
Exempt income, since crypto is not legal tender in India
Business income of the exchange that holds the wallet
questions.explanation: The 30% rule taxes gains on VDAs. Fraud proceeds merely held in USDT are unexplained money.
